analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for companies and their executives to conceal known serious product dangers from regulators, workers, and the public.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the final weeks of the 111th Congress, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, drew no cosponsors, and died without ever receiving a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the federal criminal code so that a business, or the executives and managers in charge of a product, could face up to 5 years in prison for knowing about a serious danger to their product or business practice and failing to report it to federal regulators, warn affected employees in writing, and inform other identifiable people at risk — all within 15 days of discovering it, or immediately if someone could be seriously hurt. It would also punish, with up to 1 year in prison, anyone who retaliates against an employee for reporting a danger or warning coworkers. The bill also specified that it would not preempt state law and would be interpreted to protect the public.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be consumers and workers. Consumers would gain a federal criminal backstop against companies that discover a hidden danger in a product — something not obvious to an ordinary buyer — and sit on it, because concealment would carry prison exposure for the executives responsible, not just corporate fines. Workers in plants or on product teams would be among the first to be warned in writing of serious hazards in their own workplaces, and anyone who reported a danger or warned coworkers would gain explicit criminal-law protection against being fired or otherwise punished for speaking up. State consumer-protection laws would be expressly preserved.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to 5 years in prison, for a company or its managers to know of a serious product danger and fail to report it to the appropriate federal agency, warn affected employees in writing, and inform other identifiable people at risk within 15 days (or immediately if the risk is imminent).

It creates personal criminal exposure for individual 'product supervisors' — officers, directors, partners, and managers over production, quality control, or research — rather than only corporate fines, and bars the company from paying an individual's fine for them.

It makes it a crime, punishable by up to 1 year in prison, to discriminate against an employee for reporting a product danger to a federal agency or warning coworkers, giving whistleblowers protection beyond existing civil remedies.
The bill explicitly preserves state consumer-protection laws and the right of citizens, consumers, and employees to participate in regulatory proceedings, rather than preempting them.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on manufacturers, service providers, and their executives across any industry whose products or services enter interstate commerce. Companies would face a 15-day clock to investigate and formally disclose every newly discovered serious danger to federal agencies and their own employees, under threat of criminal fines and up to 5 years' imprisonment for the company or the responsible product supervisor. Individual officers, directors, partners, and managers over production, quality control, or research would bear personal criminal liability, and the bill expressly bars the company from paying an individual's fine for them. Businesses would also bear the compliance costs of written warning systems and rapid hazard reporting.

drawbacks.text: The 15-day deadline (immediate for imminent risks) would put every company in the position of rapidly classifying newly discovered hazards under threat of a 5-year felony, which good-faith critics would say pushes firms toward over-reporting every borderline issue and could slow legitimate product development.

The bill's 'serious danger' standard turns on whether a hazard is 'not readily apparent to the average person' and could cause death or serious injury — a judgment call that would fall to individual product supervisors, exposing managers who reasonably disagree about a risk to personal criminal liability.

Applying criminal fines and prison terms to individual employees for disclosure failures is an unusually punitive approach compared with the civil penalties most product-safety law relies on, and the bill received no committee hearings where that design choice could be examined.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: today, a company that discovers its product can kill people faces regulatory penalties and lawsuits, but the people who decide to keep quiet generally face no criminal exposure, and the bill would change that while also protecting whistleblowers from retaliation. The costs are also real: a 15-day clock and a 5-year prison term attached to a judgment call about what counts as a "serious danger" invites overcautious behavior and could be applied unevenly, and the bill never got a hearing or markup where those design questions could be aired and fixed. As introduced, it was a blunt instrument aimed at a genuine problem; it died without anyone testing or refining it.

outcome.mechanism: Conyers introduced it on December 17, 2010, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. introduced the Dangerous Products Warning Act on December 17, 2010, the final stretch of the 111th Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The Judiciary Committee took no further action on the bill, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired without any action beyond its introduction and referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that discover serious dangers in their products, and the executives who decide whether to disclose them, remain free to withhold that information without criminal liability. Workers who report such dangers, and consumers exposed to hidden hazards, are no better protected than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies and executives who hid product dangers

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on December 17, 2010 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, and no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so the bill's partisan shape was never tested; the only recorded action was its introduction by a Democrat and its referral to committee.

industries.note: The bill would create criminal liability for any covered business that discovers a serious product danger and fails to disclose it to federal regulators, employees, and identifiable at-risk consumers within 15 days. Today that concealment carries regulatory and lawsuit risk; under the bill it would also carry prison exposure, which is precisely why such a bill typically draws industry resistance. Had it passed, consumers and workers would gain a legal backstop against hidden hazards.

industries.industry: Corporate officers and product supervisors (executives and managers)
industries.note: The bill attaches personal criminal liability — up to 5 years in prison — to individual officers, directors, and managers with responsibility for production, quality control, or research who sit on a known serious danger, and it bars the company from paying their fines for them. This shifts the risk of concealing product dangers from the company's balance sheet to the individuals who make the decision.
